analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent watchdog to investigate misconduct and deadly force by federal law enforcement and whistleblower protections for officers who report it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees but never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an independent Office of the Special Inspector General for Law Enforcement to investigate racial profiling, officer misconduct, use of force, and deadly force involving federal law enforcement agencies and officers. State and local governments could refer deadly-force cases to it, and states receiving federal justice grants would have to set up a process to do so. It would also protect whistleblowers who report law enforcement misconduct from retaliation. The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to a crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by or concerned about federal law enforcement misconduct, including victims of police violence and their families, would gain an independent investigator outside the Justice Department's normal chain of command. Officers who blow the whistle on misconduct would gain anti-retaliation protections and a route to court. States that comply would keep full federal grant funding while gaining an external check on local deadly-force cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of federal police misconduct; whistleblowers

how_it_helps.text: Creates an independent office to investigate racial profiling, officer misconduct, use of force, and patterns of unconstitutional misconduct by federal law enforcement.

Allows state and local agencies to refer deadly-force cases to the new office for independent investigation, with public annual reports on deadly-force cases, excessive-force complaints, and misconduct findings.
Protects law enforcement whistleblowers from retaliation, with confidentiality, court access, and anti-arbitration-clause protections.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies and officers would face independent investigations and public reporting of misconduct findings. State and local governments receiving federal justice grants would have to pass referral laws or lose Byrne and COPS grant money. Taxpayers would fund the new office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal law enforcement agencies; states lose grants

drawbacks.text: States and localities would risk losing federal justice-assistance grants (Byrne JAG and COPS funds) unless they pass laws allowing deadly-force cases to be referred for federal investigation — a condition some state and local governments would resist as federal overreach into local policing.

A new permanent federal office, with an appointed head and staff, would add to federal spending and create a new layer of investigation over agencies and officers, who would face parallel scrutiny alongside existing internal affairs and Justice Department review.

The bill shields the inspector general from easy presidential removal only by listing narrow removal grounds, and it carves out national security and ongoing-criminal-investigation matters from public reporting, which would limit how much of its work the public actually sees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would create real, independent accountability for federal law enforcement misconduct — a gap ordinary people feel directly in police shootings and profiling cases — and strong whistleblower protections. The costs are modest: a new federal office and some state compliance burdens on federal grant funds. Its weakness is that it never faced any committee action or debate, so its design was never tested. The larger problem is that nothing happened: the bill died without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee, was later sent to a crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Connolly introduced the bill on February 18, 2022, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Oversight and Reform Committee.
On November 1, 2022, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — where consideration ended.
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate before the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023.
The bill drew four cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies avoid a new independent watchdog; no member of the public gains accountability the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal law enforcement agencies; the bill died unheard

for.name: Rep. Gerald E. Connolly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a Special Inspector General for Law Enforcement.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred, keeping it from advancing.

against.name: House Oversight and Reform Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted only Democratic cosponsors (4) and never reached a vote, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies and their unions
industries.note: The bill would subject federal officers to independent external investigation of profiling, misconduct, and deadly force, and protect whistleblowers who report them. Agencies would also have to respond formally to every finding within 30 days.
The bill does not directly investigate local officers, but requires states receiving federal justice grants to set up referral processes for deadly-force cases, tying grant money to cooperation.
